description: Tectonic history of the fictional world (layer 3).

supercontinent._area_source: Cogley 1984: 210.4 M km2, 41 % of Earth's surface
supercontinent._assembly_note: final assembly ~120 Myr before breakup, as Pangaea (320 -> 200 Ma)
supercontinent._blocks_note: blocks are the continents that collided to make the supercontinent (Pangaea: ~10 major blocks); their internal sutures are older than block_complete_ma, the assembly welds run from assembly_start_ma down to assembly_age_ma

breakup._source: speeds: Zahirovic et al. 2015 (median RMS ~4 cm/yr; cratonic plates ~2.8, oceanic plates bounded by subduction ~8.5); rifting along assembly sutures, shorter ones first (Buiter & Torsvik 2014; Erdos et al. 2025)
breakup._max_age_note: the oldest ocean floor before subduction removes it; Panthalassa floor of the Jurassic was up to ~200 Myr old
breakup._micro_note: small terranes on rifted edges break away as microcontinents (Madagascar 0.59 M km2, the Seychelles bank, the Lord Howe Rise; Zealandia ~4.9 M km2 at the large end)

drift._arc_note: volcanic arcs stand ~100-300 km behind the trench (Syracuse & Abers 2006: slab depth ~100 km under the arc)
drift._merge_note: two continental plates weld once ~0.5 M km2 of crust has been consumed by their convergence; the welded plate then takes a new Euler pole by the reorganisation rule (a collision removes the slab pull between the two plates). Without the new pole, a 0.5 M km2 threshold welded every continent back into one landmass
drift._reorganisation_note: plates change their motion every few tens of Myr (Earth: global reorganisations ~100, ~83, ~50 Ma; Matthews et al. 2012); at each the Euler poles are recomputed from the configuration of that time by the same rule as at the breakup

thickness_km._source: Christensen & Mooney 1995: shields/platforms ~41 km, Palaeozoic orogens ~40, extended crust ~30, oceanic ~7; Tibet ~70 km; central Andes ~70; island arcs ~20-35 km (Izu-Bonin ~20, Aleutians ~35)

drift._arc_growth_note: magmatic addition at arcs ~30 km3 per km of arc per Myr (Reymer & Schubert 1984) spread over a ~250 km wide arc
drift._island_arc_note: arc crust forms 100-220 km behind the trench (Syracuse & Abers 2006: arc-trench distances ~100-300 km) and only where the arc stays at least 5 Myr; a band swept briefly by a migrating trench is not arc crust

post_collision._source: after the first contact, convergence goes on inside the welded plate for tens of Myr: India-Asia since ~50 Ma and still active, the Alps ~35 Myr, the Zagros ~25 Myr; Tibetan crust doubled to ~70 km and the plateau grew outwards at ~1 cm/yr. Values are order-of-magnitude

drift._accretion_note: ocean crust thicker than ~20 km (island arcs, oceanic plateaus) is too buoyant to subduct and is accreted to the continent it meets (Japan, the Cordilleran terranes, Wrangellia, the Caribbean plateau in Colombia; Cloos 1993: plateaus over ~17 km and arcs resist subduction)

output._young_note: Cenozoic events count as young orogens and active arcs, older ones as old orogens (codes of the first world)
output._shield_note: exposed shields vs covered platforms on Precambrian cratons, order of magnitude

isostasy._source: Airy isostasy, densities after Christensen & Mooney 1995; the continental surface is shifted so that the mean height of continental crust including shelves is ~120 m (Cogley 1984)

province_codes.3: old orogen (Proterozoic to Mesozoic mobile belt)

sea_level._source: Earth's ocean floor area falls about linearly with age to ~180 Myr (Parsons 1982), mean ~60 Myr; sea level change = 0.69 x change of mean basin depth (isostatic water loading; Muller et al. 2008, Science 319, 1357)

frame._note: decision 7: the spin axis moves at most 15 deg (a typical true polar wander over 100 Myr) to where the least land lies poleward of 60 deg; among axes within 0.5 % of the land of that minimum, the one nearest the simulation's axis. Without the limit the minimum (4.3 %) needed 43 deg

arc_volcanoes._source: volcanic fronts stand ~100-300 km behind the trench, typically ~150 km (Syracuse & Abers 2006); arc volcanoes are spaced ~50-70 km along the front (de Bremond d'Ars et al. 1995)

plumes._source: 49 hotspots, 7 primary (deep) ones (Courtillot et al. 2003); LIPs ~1 per 20 Myr long-term, clustered at supercontinent breakup (Bryan & Ferrari 2013); oceanic plateaus 10-35 km thick crust, Ontong Java 1.86 M km2 (Coffin & Eldholm 1994); Hawaiian swell ~1 km high, half-width ~500 km (Van Ark & Lin 2004)
plumes._count_note: secondary plumes live 10-60 Myr, so ~1/3 of them are active at any time: 90 give ~30 active, plus 7 primary, close to Earth's ~40-49 hotspots today
plumes._drift_note: hotspots move slowly in the mantle: primary ones by ~1 cm/yr or less within a hemisphere; up to 5 cm/yr between hemispheres before 50 Ma (Courtillot et al. 2003)
plumes._spacing_note: volcanoes along the Hawaiian chain stand ~40-60 km apart (ten Brink 1991); weaker tracks are sparser
plumes._flood_note: continental flood basalts are ~1-3 km of lava (Deccan up to ~2 km) plus underplating; +3 km of crust gives ~+430 m by Airy, like the Deccan plateau (~0.5-1 km); lavas thin over the outer ~250 km
